episode_title: A push to ban slaughter without stunning, Verstappen wins again, and Van Dijk hits 100
description: Animal welfare state secretary Silvio Erkens says the Netherlands should follow Belgium and ban slaughter without stunning, which reopens a 15-year fight over religious freedom. We also cover Verstappen's first win of the season after a chaotic start, Van Dijk's 100th game for Oranje, and Damen's multi-billion claim against Germany over cancelled warships. Then the future of the Delta Works, Polymarket's court fight and Michelin's 100th birthday, plus what's on in Amsterdam today.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A junior minister wants to ban slaughtering animals without stunning them first, and Jewish groups are already vowing to fight it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Plus a big sporting weekend. Max Verstappen finally wins a race, and Virgil van Dijk plays his hundredth game for Oranje.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Monday, the fifth of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

segments.title: A push to ban slaughter without stunning

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start with a debate that's been running here for fifteen years: slaughtering animals without stunning them first.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's back because of Silvio Erkens. He's the staatssecretaris, the state secretary, for agriculture. That's a junior minister, and animal welfare is his area. He's from the VVD, the center-right liberals.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: On Sunday, which was World Animal Day, he told the TV programme WNL op Zondag that slaughter without stunning "does not belong in the Netherlands," and that it's time to lift the taboo around it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So what actually happens now?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A certified slaughterer cuts the animal's throat with a razor-sharp knife. If it isn't dead within forty seconds, it has to be stunned. Erkens called that "forty seconds of animal suffering."

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The exception is there for religious reasons. Some Islamic and Jewish rules say the animal has to be alive and conscious when it's slaughtered. Some groups do accept a temporary, reversible stun, because the animal is still alive when it's cut.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: How many animals are we talking about?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: De Telegraaf says about twenty-six thousand in 2024. The vast majority were sheep and goats.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Erkens isn't writing a law himself, though.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No, he's backing someone else's. The Partij voor de Dieren, the Party for the Animals, is a small animal-rights party. It's filing a bill this month, written by its MP Esther Ouwehand, and Erkens says the cabinet looks on it favourably.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And they've tried this before.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In 2011. That bill passed the Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives. Then the Eerste Kamer, the Senate, voted it down, because a majority there said it violated freedom of religion.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So what's changed?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Two things. First, the new bill goes much further. It would also ban gassing pigs with CO2 to stun them, electric water baths for poultry and tipping poultry out of crates. And it would bar slaughtering animals that are more than forty percent of the way through a pregnancy. Second, Europe. The Raad van State, the Council of State, is the government's top legal adviser, and last year it was largely positive about the bill. It said recent European rulings leave more room to put animal welfare ahead of religious freedom.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Those rulings were about Belgium. Flanders and Wallonia both ban slaughter without stunning. The EU Court of Justice backed their bans in 2020, and the European Court of Human Rights did the same in 2024.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Even so, Erkens stresses that any law has to hold up legally. He also rejects the idea that it targets Muslims. He says ritual slaughter with stunning would still be allowed, and about half of ritual slaughter here already happens that way. And he points out that Denmark, Belgium, Greece and Austria already have bans.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Jewish organisations are angry. Hans Weijel, vice-chairman of the Central Jewish Council, called it "another blow against Jews." He said the council will coordinate its opposition with Muslim organisations.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And where do the parties stand?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: When the Council of State gave its advice, the far-right PVV, the VVD, D66, GroenLinks-PvdA and the SP all backed a ban. The Christian Democrats of the CDA have been sceptical. And two small parties defend religious freedom on this: the orthodox Protestant SGP, and DENK, which has a largely Muslim base.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So the bill arrives this month. If it gets through the House, the Senate gets the final say again.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Max Verstappen has finally won a race this season, and just getting to the start line was half the drama.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Half? More like all of it. For starters, it was the Bahrain Grand Prix. Held in Malaysia.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Naturally.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The April races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled over the security situation in the Middle East, so this one moved to the Sepang circuit. Then rain, thunder and lightning delayed the start. And on the formation laps, about eight cars just lost power and stopped. Including Verstappen's.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They just stopped? All at the same time?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It was a software fault. The FIA, the sport's governing body, said the software hadn't been tested in wet, slow conditions like these. The fix was an update that took about twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So the fastest cars in the world were sitting there waiting for a software update. Very relatable.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The FIA apologised to fans and promised a full review. No penalties so far. The race started an hour and a half late.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And Max?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He started from pole on intermediates, the light-rain tyres, while lots of rivals gambled on dry tyres. He got away badly and dropped behind both Mercedes. Then he passed George Russell on lap six. As the track dried, Red Bull made a bold call and put him on softs, and he took the lead from championship leader Kimi Antonelli at a safety car restart. He won by two point three seconds, with Lewis Hamilton third.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's been a rough year for him, hasn't it?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He's a four-time world champion, and he's sixth in the standings. This is his first win since Abu Dhabi last December, and Red Bull's first with the engine it now builds itself. He celebrated with his dad, Jos, who used to race in F1 himself.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Singapore's next weekend. Antonelli can't wrap up the title there, but he could at the US Grand Prix on the twenty-fifth. For one Sunday, though, the fans in orange got their moment.

segments.title: Van Dijk's 100th as Oranje beat Serbia

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Staying with orange: the national football team beat Serbia on a big night for their captain.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Virgil van Dijk played his hundredth game for Oranje. He's only the eleventh Dutch man to get there. He walked out in Eindhoven holding his son Mase's hand, and he said he'd been emotional in the dressing room.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And then they played him on the right, which isn't his usual spot. Happy anniversary, here's a new job.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He says he won't stop at a hundred. He's thirty-five, and he's committed to playing through Euro 2028.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The record belongs to Wesley Sneijder, with a hundred and thirty-four. So he'd better keep going.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: As for the game, it finished two-one in the Nations League. Teun Koopmeiners curled a free kick straight in. Four minutes later, Serbia's nineteen-year-old Mihajlo Cvetković headed in the equaliser.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's twelve games in a row now where Oranje have conceded, if you're keeping count.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The substitute Joshua Zirkzee tapped in the winner in the seventy-first minute, after Tijjani Reijnders laid the ball back across goal. Who sent in the cross is disputed. Most reports say Denzel Dumfries, but NOS says Crysencio Summerville.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And they finished with ten men?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They'd used all their subs when Micky van de Ven hurt his hand late on. Serbia's Luka Jović stepped on it in a challenge. It's not clear yet how serious it is, and that's a worry for his club, Tottenham.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The new bondscoach, the national team coach, is Xavi Hernández, the former Barcelona midfielder and coach. This was his first set of matches in charge: two wins, two draws, no losses. By the end he'd lost his voice, and he said the team is "forging a family."

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Dutch and Greece are level on points and goal difference, but the Dutch are listed first because they've scored more. They play again in November: Greece at home, then Germany away.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Next, a Dutch shipbuilder is sending Germany a very big bill.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Damen, a family-owned Dutch firm and one of Europe's biggest shipbuilders, is claiming nearly four point seven billion euros from the German government.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: For what?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Six F126 frigates, which are mid-sized warships. Germany ordered them and then cancelled. It was one of the largest naval orders a Dutch company has ever won.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why did Berlin pull out?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Defence minister Boris Pistorius ended it in June. He pointed to years of delays, and he said the projected cost had gone from about ten billion euros to more than eighteen. Germany's buying eight frigates from the German shipbuilder ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems instead.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And Damen says that's on Germany.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It blames the German government for the delays and calls the cancellation a politically motivated breach of contract. Four point three billion of the claim is for materials that were already ordered, and much of that is owed to subcontractors. Damen may also claim more damages on top.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Let me guess. Germany disagrees.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Pistorius called it a "prophylactic counter-attack." He says Damen performed poorly, and that Germany may file counterclaims of up to two point three billion euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So where does this end up?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's not clear yet. So far it's just letters from Damen's lawyer to the German defence ministry and to members of committees in the Bundestag, the German parliament. No court case or arbitration has been reported.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And is Belgium watching this too?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Very closely. Belgium's two frigates are part of a joint Dutch-Belgian order with Damen. Belgian defence minister Theo Francken has been looking at other suppliers because of delays and rising costs, and an internal navy evaluation reportedly favours an Italian frigate. He's said he'll decide this month.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So October could turn out to be an expensive month for Damen.

segments.title: The Delta Works at 40, and rising seas

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, the Delta Works, and how long they can keep the sea out.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This started as a birthday story, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sunday was forty years since Queen Beatrix opened the Oosterscheldekering, the storm surge barrier in Zeeland, the southwestern coastal province.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Some quick context. The Deltawerken, the Delta Works, are a huge system of dams, sluices and storm barriers. They were built after the 1953 North Sea flood, which killed more than eighteen hundred people. The Oosterschelde barrier is the famous one. Its gates only close during storms, and that kept the estuary's tidal ecosystem alive.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It was meant to last about two hundred years. It won't.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Because of sea level rise?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's part of it. Rijkswaterstaat, the national water agency, calculates the barrier hits its limit at around sixty centimetres of sea level rise. By then it would have to close about ten times a year, which is the most it can handle while still being maintained. Right now it closes about once a year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So when does it need replacing?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A government programme on sea level rise, finished in June, expects the Oosterschelde and Maeslant barriers to need replacing between 2070 and 2100, mainly because they're wearing out.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: 2070 sounds like ages away.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Except one expert says building a replacement takes about forty years.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ah. So the clock's already running.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There are three options. They could raise the water level at which the gates close, but then the dikes would need strengthening too. They could rebuild the barrier. Or they could replace it with a permanent dam. Delta Commissioner Co Verdaas says the decision can't wait another twenty years.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In a country where so much of the land is below sea level, that's not an abstract debate.

segments.title: Polymarket takes its Dutch ban to court

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, the prediction site Polymarket is going to court to fight its ban in the Netherlands.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Wait, what's a prediction market?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's a site where users trade contracts that pay out depending on whether an event happens. Polymarket is a big American one.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Sounds like betting.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's what the Kansspelautoriteit, the Dutch Gambling Authority, decided in February. It ruled that Polymarket was a gambling site with no licence and ordered it to stop operating here, or face a penalty of four hundred and twenty thousand euros a week. Polymarket did stop, but too late, so it had to pay that four hundred and twenty thousand once.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And now it's told the financial daily FD that it's going to court.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It'll argue this isn't a game of chance, it's a financial product, like futures. That would put it under the AFM, the financial markets regulator.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Does the AFM agree?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It hasn't taken a public position. But in July the EU markets watchdog, ESMA, weighed in. It said only event contracts tied to things like indices, currencies or commodity prices count as financial instruments, and those fall under the EU ban on selling binary options to ordinary investors. Critics say Polymarket's contracts look a lot like binary options anyway.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So even if it wins the argument, it might still lose. And it's not just a Dutch fight. It's banned in France and Germany too, and in the US, prediction markets are fighting over the same question: gambling or finance?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Polymarket is lobbying in Brussels to be treated as a financial product across the EU. There's no word yet on a hearing date here.

segments.title: Amsterdam-Noord school director hired family firms

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here in Amsterdam, a school director in Noord is under scrutiny over the firms he hired.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Het Parool, the Amsterdam daily, reports that a school director in Amsterdam-Noord, across the IJ from the city centre, hired small companies owned by his daughter and his son-in-law. In total he paid them nearly a million euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why does that matter beyond one school?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Because Dutch schools are almost entirely publicly funded. School boards have to account for that money, and the Inspectie van het Onderwijs, the Education Inspectorate, oversees them. Hiring family firms without an open tender raises questions about conflicts of interest.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What don't we know yet?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Quite a lot. The school hasn't been publicly named, and it's not clear what work the companies did or over what period. There's also no word yet on whether the school board or the Inspectorate has stepped in, or on what the director has to say.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: We'll keep an eye on that one.

segments.title: Poll: most Dutch people oppose slavery reparations

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, the country's slavery past, and a new poll on reparations.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: On Friday we told you about the study showing the House of Orange-Nassau supported colonialism and slavery for centuries, and about Prime Minister Rob Jetten ruling out new reparations.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: An RTL poll suggests most people are with him. Eighty-three percent said the Netherlands shouldn't pay reparations. Eight percent said it should.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Is there a split by party?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A sharp one. Among voters for the right-wing parties, the PVV, VVD, JA21, BBB and FvD, ninety-nine percent are opposed. So are seventy-one percent of voters for Jetten's own party, D66. GroenLinks-PvdA supporters are split right down the middle.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And how much attention should the colonial past get?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Thirty-eight percent say it already gets too much, though most say the current level is about right or could be higher. There's an age gap too. Twenty-four percent of younger respondents say it gets too little attention, compared with six percent of people over sixty-five.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's not yet clear how many people took part, or exactly how the question was worded.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Michelin star day, Sam, and somewhere a restaurant is very nervous about a table for one.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why a table for one?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Because inspectors mostly eat alone. Château Neercanne in Maastricht was one of the first Dutch restaurants to get a star, back in 1957, and its staff say solo bookings make them nervous.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Fair enough. So the big announcement is today?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The new Dutch stars are being announced today at the MECC in Maastricht. And it's a centenary, too. The first stars were given out in France in 1926.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: By a tyre company, to get people driving to restaurants. Honestly, marketing genius.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Werner Loens, a former director of Michelin Benelux, spent thirty-seven years as an inspector and head inspector. He's eaten in eight and a half thousand restaurants in twenty-two countries.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Where do I apply?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's about two hundred and fifty restaurant meals a year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Where do I un-apply?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They also book under common fake names. In the Netherlands, his was Jan Jansen.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Dutch John Smith. Nobody would ever suspect a thing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And no star comes from a single visit. A promising place gets three or four more, months apart. Inspectors judge the ingredients, the technique, the harmony, the personality and the consistency, and Loens says consistency is the hardest.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Three stars are for places where, in his words, "craft becomes art." Going into today, only De Librije in Zwolle had three in the Netherlands.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: For the rest of us, there's the Bib Gourmand, Michelin's award for good food at a moderate price. Amsterdam got three new ones last week: FuLu Mandarijn on the Rokin, Utage Sake Bar in Zuid, and Boon & De Koot in West.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now that's a list I can afford to eat my way through. And if dinner's sorted, there's plenty to do around it today.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Tonight at seven thirty, the Brazilian band Azymuth plays the Melkweg in the Leidsebuurt. They've been mixing jazz, funk and samba for more than fifty years. Bassist Alex Malheiros, the only original member left, leads the show.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: MF Doom and Flying Lotus have sampled them, so you may know their music without knowing it. If you're free in the daytime, ARTIS Aquarium at the zoo in the Plantage has Olafur Eliasson's Deep Seeing Currents, from nine till five. It's a dark room full of whale song and deep-sea rumbling, with 3D sound you can feel in your body. It's part of the Amsterdam Dance Event's daytime programme, and you don't need any Dutch.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And at LAB111 in Oud-West, there's Charlie Chaplin's The Great Dictator, the first film where he speaks. It's a 1940 satire of Nazi Germany, and it's showing until Friday.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's it for today. I'm Sam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And I'm Maya. Thanks for listening to Dutch Daily Briefing. See you tomorrow.
